deep.reconstruction:
Notation: ∫1/z^m means ζ(m) = Σ_{z≥1} z^{-m}. ∫1/z^m (1/y^n) means S(m,n) = Σ_z z^{-m} H_z^{(n)}, where H_z^{(n)} = Σ_{y≤z} y^{-n}; in modern terms S(m,n) = ζ(m,n) + ζ(m+n). The paper derives relations among these 'Euler sums' in two ways. The 'first method' is the elementary symmetric relation S(m,n) + S(n,m) = ζ(m)ζ(n) + ζ(m+n), i.e. the stuffle (harmonic product) relation. The 'second method' comes from partial fractions; it is essentially the shuffle-type relation (Euler's decomposition formula) for ζ(m)ζ(n) − ζ(m+n).

Order three (weight 4), case m=3, n=1. The second method gives ζ(3)ζ(1) − ζ(4) = S(3,1) − 2ζ(2)² + S(1,3) + S(2,2) + S(3,1). The divergent terms 2ζ(3)ζ(1) have already cancelled. Hence 2S(3,1) + S(2,2) + S(1,3) = 2ζ(2)² + ζ(3)ζ(1) − ζ(4). Subtracting the stuffle relation S(3,1) + S(1,3) = ζ(3)ζ(1) + ζ(4) gives S(3,1) + S(2,2) = 2ζ(2)² − 2ζ(4).

Case m=n=2. The second method gives ζ(2)² − ζ(4) = 2[2ζ(2)² − S(2,2) − 2S(3,1)], so 2S(2,2) + 4S(3,1) = 3ζ(2)² + ζ(4). The stuffle relation gives 2S(2,2) = ζ(2)² + ζ(4). Therefore S(2,2) = ½ζ(2)² + ½ζ(4) and S(3,1) = ½ζ(2)².

The divergent case then yields S(3,1) = (3/2)ζ(2)² − (5/2)ζ(4). The next page shows this agrees with the convergent case because ζ(2)² = π⁴/36 = (5/2)ζ(4). Euler concludes that cancelling a single divergent ζ(1) is harmless, and that errors occur only when ζ(1)² enters, as in order one. In modern terms: ζ(3,1) = π⁴/360 and ζ(2,2) = (ζ(2)² − ζ(4))/2 = 3π⁴/360. The page is part of Euler's systematic weight-by-weight derivation of double zeta values. It serves to establish closed forms for the Euler sums and to test the reliability of manipulating divergent ζ(1).
errors: No mathematical errors. All four printed equations check numerically: S(3,1) = π⁴/72 and S(2,2) = 7π⁴/360. The step relies on formal cancellation of the divergent ζ(1) terms, which Euler acknowledges on the previous and next pages.

missed.claim: Euler's empirical diagnosis has a precise modern form. He observes that formal cancellation of divergent ζ(1) gives true relations when ζ(1) enters only linearly (orders two and three), but fails when ζ(1)² appears (order one). This exactly mirrors the Ihara–Kaneko–Zagier theorem: the shuffle- and stuffle-regularizations differ by the map ρ, whose correction terms begin at T² with ζ(2) (ζ(1,1) gives T²/2 versus (T²−ζ(2))/2). So Euler's 'naive' regularized double shuffle is valid precisely in the regime IKZ identify. Historical accounts usually credit Euler with the relations but rarely with this criterion for when divergent manipulation is safe.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This gives Euler explicit priority for a heuristic form of regularized double shuffle and its limitation at degree ≥2 in the divergence. It is a nice historical anchor for the IKZ comparison map.

deep.surprise_reason: The results themselves are well known and credited to E477. What is mildly notable is Euler's explicit test of divergent cancellations and his correct criterion: linear divergence is fine, the square of the divergence is not. This matches regularization theory, but the link may already be remarked in the MZV literature.
transcription_corrections: In the first displayed expression, the final term is printed faintly. It must read ∫1/z³(1/y), not ∫1/z⁴(1/y), for the stated consequence 2S(3,1)+S(2,2)+S(1,3)=… to follow.
Coefficients in 'vnde concludimus fore' are ½ and ½ (printed as small fractions), and in the last line 3/2 and 5/2. The transcription is correct on these points.
